title: Primary Amenorrhoea in a 17-Year-Old
patient_instructions: You are Karen, the mother of Emily, a 17-year-old student who has not yet had her first period. You are worried something is seriously wrong. Emily is with you but you are doing the talking. Emily developed breasts from about age 11 and has normal underarm and pubic hair and had a growth spurt - so she has clearly gone through puberty, she just has never bled. She has no monthly cramping abdominal pain. She is a virgin and not sexually active. She does not exercise excessively, is not dieting, has not lost weight, and eats normally. No headaches, no vision problems, no milky nipple discharge. No heat or cold intolerance. No acne or excessive facial/body hair. She takes no medications and has no medical problems. You (the mother) started your periods at 15, and Emily's older sister started at 14. IDEAS: 'Is she infertile? Does she have a genetic problem?' CONCERNS: that she is abnormal. EXPECTATIONS: to find out why and what needs to be done. Affect: anxious but cooperative. If the candidate is reassuring and explains constitutional delay clearly, you are relieved. On the screen the physical examination shows Tanner stage 5, no imperforate hymen; an internal (speculum/bimanual) examination is not appropriate as she is a virgin.
candidate_instructions: You are a GP. A mother brings her 17-year-old daughter Emily, who has never had a period. Take a focused history from the mother (the examination findings appear on screen: Tanner stage 5, no imperforate hymen). In 8 minutes: take the history, then explain your provisional diagnosis and differentials to the mother. Note this is an adolescent case; consider consent and the presence of a parent.
examiner_instructions: The candidate should define primary amenorrhoea and, given normal secondary sexual characteristics (Tanner 5) with absent menarche, work through an upper-to-lower differential: hypothalamic (stress, excessive exercise, eating disorder, weight loss), pituitary (hypopituitarism, prolactinoma), thyroid, ovarian (Turner syndrome, POI), PCOS, structural (Mullerian agenesis/MRKH, imperforate hymen) and constitutional delay. With normal puberty, no cyclical pain, no excessive exercise/weight loss, and a family history of late menarche, the best-fit is constitutional delay (a diagnosis of exclusion). Candidate should NOT perform a bimanual/speculum examination in a virgin adolescent (critical error). Reward mention of first-line investigations (beta-hCG, FSH/LH, oestradiol, TSH, prolactin, pelvic ultrasound; karyotype if hypergonadotropic). Prompt if needed: 'What is your most likely diagnosis and why?'

criteria: Clarifies pubertal development (thelarche, adrenarche, growth spurt) to separate primary amenorrhoea from delayed puberty
Screens hypothalamic causes (stress, excessive exercise, diet/weight loss, eating disorder) and asks about cyclical abdominal pain (imperforate hymen)
Screens pituitary/thyroid/ovarian/PCOS clues (headache, visual change, galactorrhoea, heat/cold intolerance, acne, hirsutism)
Takes family history of late menarche/genetic conditions and asks age-appropriate sensitive questions with consent
Reaches constitutional delay as most likely given normal Tanner 5 development and supportive family history
Frames it as a diagnosis of exclusion and structures a differential using the upper-to-lower approach
Distinguishes primary amenorrhoea from delayed puberty (absent secondary sexual characteristics)
Proposes first-line investigations (beta-hCG, FSH/LH, oestradiol, TSH, prolactin, pelvic ultrasound; karyotype if hypergonadotropic)
Avoids inappropriate bimanual/speculum examination in a virgin adolescent and considers consent/Gillick competence
Plans appropriate referral (paediatric endocrinology/gynaecology) if a structural, ovarian or pituitary cause is found, with reassurance/safety-net
Explains diagnosis and differentials to the mother in lay terms, addresses fears and checks understanding

red_flags: Absent secondary sexual characteristics (no thelarche) by age 13 - mandates earlier endocrine/genetic workup for delayed puberty
Cyclical lower abdominal pain with primary amenorrhoea and normal development - suggests outflow obstruction (imperforate hymen/haematocolpos)
Hypergonadotropic picture (high FSH/LH) - karyotype to detect Turner syndrome (45,X)
Headache, visual field defect or galactorrhoea - exclude a prolactinoma/pituitary lesion
Signs of an eating disorder or the female athlete triad requiring targeted assessment
australian_guidelines: RANZCOG/eTG threshold: investigate primary amenorrhoea when menses have not started by age 15 with normal secondary sexual development, or by age 13 with no development

2023 International Evidence-Based PCOS Guideline (RANZCOG/ESHRE-endorsed): do NOT use pelvic ultrasound to diagnose PCOS within 8 years of menarche - multifollicular ovaries are physiological in adolescence; the polycystic morphology threshold is >=20 follicles/ovary or ovarian volume >=10 mL
First-line investigation pathway: urine/serum beta-hCG, FSH/LH, oestradiol, TSH, prolactin and pelvic ultrasound, then karyotype if hypergonadotropic to detect Turner syndrome
Adolescent care: ensure a parent/guardian is present, consider Gillick/mature-minor competence, and do not perform a speculum/bimanual examination in a virgin adolescent
learning_objectives: Distinguish primary amenorrhoea from delayed puberty using pubertal staging
Construct an upper-to-lower differential for primary amenorrhoea
Select first-line investigations and know when karyotyping and referral are indicated
Apply adolescent consent principles and avoid inappropriate intimate examination
key_points: Constitutional delay is a diagnosis of exclusion, appropriate only after normal examination and investigations
Mullerian agenesis (MRKH) is congenital absence of the uterus and upper vagina, a structural cause of primary amenorrhoea
Ultrasound should not be used to diagnose PCOS in an adolescent within 8 years of menarche
A bimanual/speculum examination in a virgin adolescent is contraindicated

citations.claim: Amenorrhoea is classified as primary or secondary, and the key task in primary amenorrhoea is differentiating it from delayed puberty where there are no signs of sexual maturation.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2548

citations.claim: Delayed puberty / constitutional delay is a recognised variant of normal within the differential of failure of sexual maturation, alongside central and systemic causes.
citations.source: AMC Anthology of Medical Conditions.pdf, p.357

citations.claim: PCOS is a leading ovarian cause of androgen excess producing hirsutism and acne, supporting PCOS screening questions.
citations.source: AMC Anthology of Medical Conditions.pdf, p.203

citations.claim: Hyperprolactinaemia (prolactinoma) is treated with dopamine agonists and PCOS-related anovulation with metformin - relevant to the prolactinoma and PCOS differentials.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2790
